title: Hobbes Publishes Leviathan and Makes the Case for an Undivided Sovereign
dek: In 1651, as England's civil wars end, Thomas Hobbes publishes Leviathan in London, arguing that only one undivided sovereign power can keep people from a war of all against all.
body: He wrote it in Paris among exiled royalists. The book cost him their favour, and that winter he went home to London and the new republic.

panels.label: Hobbes Argued
panels.text: Hobbes argued that without a common power people live in a war of every man against every man, so they must give one undivided sovereign their obedience for as long as it can protect them.

panels.label: His Critics Argued
panels.text: Republicans such as James Harrington argued that a free state is an empire of laws, not of men, and Anglicans such as Bishop John Bramhall argued that his materialism led toward atheism.

panels.label: The Stakes
panels.text: Both camps wanted an end to civil war; at stake was whether peace required one undivided power over Church and state, or rule bound by law and by the Church’s own authority.
